notable_absence.finding: This page directly answers the round's open question about whether XATTRs constitute a third/fourth access-grant mechanism alongside admin_channels (REST), access()/role() (sync function), and legacy config. They do not: the page's own three-step structure (Configuration -> Setting -> Use in a Sync Function) shows the XATTR is purely an alternative DATA SOURCE feeding the pre-existing channel()/access()/role() sync-function calls - 'Access grant information such as Channels and Roles can be derived or specified as a property within the document body... Alternatively, a more secure option is to store this information in user XATTRs.' The grant mechanism itself is unchanged (still channel()/access()/role() executing inside the sync function); only where the argument value comes FROM changes (document body property vs. meta.xattrs.<name>). What IS structurally new, and has no counterpart anywhere else in the batch, is the WRITE PATH for that data: it must be set via a Couchbase Server Key-Value SDK sub-document call (LookupIn/MutateIn with isXattr:true) against the underlying bucket - a write surface entirely outside Sync Gateway's own Admin REST API, config file, or sync-function surfaces. This means the access-grant metadata for XATTR-based routing is provisioned by a THIRD PRODUCT SURFACE (the Couchbase Server SDK, operating on the Server bucket underneath Sync Gateway) that Sync Gateway itself has no write access to at all - not a third grant mechanism, but a write-path dependency on a different product's API for the data one specific transport option relies on.

cross_component_finding: The stated motivation for XATTR-based routing is a genuine, quantified security/architecture trade-off unique to this mechanism in the whole batch: 'It provide an added level of security, users can no longer identify the channels and users a document is available to by reading its contents, because the information is in metadata that is inaccessible to them' and 'Separation of concerns. By separating access grant metadata from document contents, changes to access grants will not create a new document revision that is subsequently pushed to a client.' The second point is a direct callback to the batch's revocation/auto-purge findings: because access grants ordinarily live IN the document body (read by channel()/access()), changing them creates a new revision that must itself be synced and re-evaluated by every replica; routing that data through XATTR metadata instead means an access-grant change does not itself generate synced document traffic - it only changes what the (separately-triggered) sync function computes the next time it runs. No equivalent 'does changing the access grant itself generate replicated traffic' concern exists in server/'s or Capella's models, since neither replicates a privilege/role change to end-client devices the way SGW replicates document revisions to Couchbase Lite.
